::: {#rem-surprisal-log-rarity}
#### Surprisal is the logarithm of the rarity

The [surprisal](#def-surprisal) of an [outcome](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-experiment-outcome) $x$ is the [logarithm](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm) of its [rarity](#def-rarity):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\surprisalf{x}
&= -\logf{\P(X=x)} \\
&= \logf{\frac{1}{\P(X=x)}} \\
&= \logf{\rarityf{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For a [discrete random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-discrete-rv),
the rarity is at least $1$,
with equality exactly when $\P(X=x) = 1$,
so the surprisal is never below $0$.
For a [continuous random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-continuous-rv),
the same equalities hold with the [density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf) in place of the mass:
$\surprisalf{x} = -\logf{\p(x)} = \logf{\rarityf{x}}$.
A density can exceed $1$, so there the rarity can be below $1$.
For a mass, a rarity of $r$ reads "one in $r$":
an outcome with rarity $4$ has [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $1/4$ and a surprisal of $2$ [bits](#def-bit).

:::
